belongs_to: "What do the numbers in the figure below tell us?" - first line-up of 7 stick-figure children with number speech bubbles
description: Seven coloured stick-figure children stand in one row, left to right, facing the same way, each with a light-blue speech bubble above the head holding one number. Heights differ. Left to right (colour of the stick figure, height rank 1 = shortest ... 7 = tallest, number in the bubble): 1st light blue, rank 5, bubble 0; 2nd olive-yellow, rank 1 (shortest), bubble 1; 3rd red, rank 7 (tallest), bubble 0; 4th orange, rank 2, bubble 2; 5th mustard-yellow, rank 3, bubble 2; 6th purple, rank 4, bubble 2; 7th green, rank 6, bubble 1. So the bubbles read 0, 1, 0, 2, 2, 2, 1 and the height ranks read 5, 1, 7, 2, 3, 4, 6 (rank order read from the top of each head; each bubble matches the book's rule 'number of children in front who are taller'). Each line-up stands in front of 11 equally spaced thin light-grey horizontal ruled lines (counted: 11); the bottom ruled line is the ground line and every child's feet rest on it. The bubbles sit at different heights, each just above its child's head, tail pointing down to the head.

Each line-up stands in front of 11 equally spaced thin light-grey horizontal ruled lines (counted: 11); the bottom ruled line is the ground line and every child's feet rest on it. Same drawing style as the first line-up (bubble just above each head).

belongs_to: Kishor's puzzle: "There are 5 boxes, and each box should contain exactly 1 number card. The numbers in the boxes should sum to 30."
description: A single row of five EMPTY white rectangular boxes (black outline, landscape rectangles, equal size) joined by four plus signs: [ ] + [ ] + [ ] + [ ] + [ ] = 30. The text '= 30' follows the fifth box. No numbers inside any box.

belongs_to: Kishor's number cards: "Can you figure out which 5 cards add to 30? Is it possible? There are many ways of choosing 5 cards from this collection."
description: Seven small piles of square number cards in a row under the five boxes, each pile one colour and one number, cards slightly rotated and overlapping, each card with a thin black outline and its number printed in dark ink. Left to right (counted): purple cards '13' x 3 cards; pink/salmon cards '9' x 4 cards; dark-green cards '1' x 3 cards (top one partly covered); yellow cards '7' x 4 cards; light-green cards '11' x 3 cards; orange/peach cards '5' x 4 cards; light-blue cards '3' x 4 cards. Total 25 cards; all numbers are odd (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13).

belongs_to: "Any even number can be arranged in pairs without any leftovers. Some even numbers are shown here, arranged in pairs."
description: Three groups of identical pink (magenta) round dots side by side, each dot set in pairs: (1) a vertical block of 3 rows x 2 columns = 6 dots; (2) a tilted strip of 5 pairs (each pair a short row of 2 dots, rows stepping down to the left from top right to bottom left) = 10 dots; (3) a horizontal block of 2 rows x 9 columns = 18 dots. No leftover single dot in any group (6, 10 and 18 are even).

belongs_to: "As we see in the figure, adding any number of even numbers will result in a number which can still be arranged in pairs" - small picture beside this text
description: A single block of round dots, 2 columns x 5 rows = 10 dots, printed to the right of the paragraph. Top 3 rows (6 dots) are green, bottom 2 rows (4 dots) are purple. It shows two even numbers (6 green + 4 purple) joined, still all in pairs.

belongs_to: "An odd number is one more than a collection of pairs. Some odd numbers are shown below:"
description: Three groups of dots side by side, each made of pink pairs plus ONE extra dark navy-blue dot: (1) a vertical block of 3 rows x 2 columns of pink dots (6) with one navy dot below the left column = 7 dots; (2) a tilted strip of 10 pink dots in pairs (5 pairs, stepping down to the right from top left to bottom right) with one navy dot at the bottom end = 11 dots; (3) a horizontal block of 2 rows x 9 pink dots (18) with one navy dot at the right end of the bottom row = 19 dots. The navy dot is the unpaired leftover in each.

belongs_to: "This figure shows that the sum of two odd numbers must always be even!" - picture at the top right of the page
description: One block of round dots, 2 columns x 6 rows = 12 dots, printed to the right of the paragraph. Green dots: the first 3 rows (6 dots) plus the left dot of row 4 = 7 green. Purple dots: the right dot of row 4 plus rows 5 and 6 (4 dots) = 5 purple. So 7 + 5 = 12: the two leftover single dots (one green, one purple) sit together in row 4 and form a pair.

belongs_to: Boy's speech bubble: "We can see that two odd numbers added together can always be arranged in pairs." - three dot blocks next to the boy
description: Three blocks of 2-column dot arrays of increasing height, bottoms aligned, left to right (green + purple dots, rows of 2): (1) 3 rows = 6 dots: 3 green (row 1 both, row 2 left) + 3 purple (row 2 right, row 3 both); (2) 4 rows = 8 dots: 5 green (rows 1 and 2 both, row 3 left) + 3 purple (row 3 right, row 4 both); (3) 6 rows = 12 dots: 3 green (row 1 both, row 2 left) + 9 purple (row 2 right, rows 3 to 6 both). In each array the two odd numbers (green and purple) are joined and every dot has a partner. The boy cartoon and speech bubble beside it are decoration; the bubble text is the sentence quoted above.

Printed beside a photograph of the stone inscription (the photograph itself, a dark stone slab with carved numerals in a 4 x 4 grid, is not drawn as a figure here); caption under both: 'The first ever recorded 4 x 4 magic square, the Chautisa Yantra, at Khajuraho, India'.

belongs_to: "Magic Squares in History and Culture": the Lo Shu legend - "The turtle carried a 3 x 3 grid on its back, with the numbers 1 to 9 arranged in a magical pattern."
description: A top-down drawing of a green turtle with a black shell divided by white lines into a ring of 8 segments around a central round segment (3 x 3 pattern). Each of the 9 segments carries white dots (or small hollow circles) in a pattern, standing for the numbers 1 to 9: centre = 5 dots in a plus shape; bottom segment = 1 dot; left segment = 3 dots in a vertical line; top-right segment = 2 dots in a short diagonal; top-left segment = a small ring/diamond of dots (4); bottom-right and bottom-left segments = tilted 2-column dot strips (6 and 8); top segment and right segment = triangle-shaped dot clusters (9 and 7). The pattern is the Lo Shu square 4 9 2 / 3 5 7 / 8 1 6 (top-left to bottom-right), which is a different orientation from the printed number grid P12-grid-2.
unclear: Dot counts per segment are tiny and low resolution; the numbers 9, 7, 4, 6, 8 are inferred from the Lo Shu arrangement and a rough look, not counted dot by dot.
Mostly an illustration of the legend; the question-relevant version is the printed number grid P12-grid-2.

belongs_to: "The first magic square ever recorded, the Lo Shu Square" - printed number grid on the left of the text
description: A 3 x 3 grid with red outline and red lines, white cells, numbers: row 1: 2, 7, 6; row 2: 9, 5, 1; row 3: 4, 3, 8. Every row, column and diagonal adds to 15. Printed at the left margin beside the Lo Shu paragraph.

belongs_to: "The Navagraha Yantra is one such example shown below."
description: A square board with a thick black border, split into a 3 x 3 arrangement of nine coloured panels separated by black lines. Each panel has the graha's name in white serif letters at the top and, in the middle, a 3 x 3 magic square inside a themed shape. Row 1, left to right: Mercury (dark green panel; cream-coloured 3x3 square with a cream arrow shape pointing out at the top-left and another at the bottom-right): 9 4 11 / 10 8 6 / 5 12 7. Venus (lavender panel; cream six-pointed star (hexagram) with the square in its middle): 11 6 13 / 12 10 8 / 7 14 9. Moon (khaki/brown panel; cream ring/circle holding the square): 7 2 9 / 8 6 4 / 3 10 5. Row 2: Jupiter (olive-brown panel; cream square frame with small corner curls): 10 5 12 / 11 9 7 / 6 13 8. Sun (mustard-yellow panel; red sun with rays around a cream circle holding the square): 6 1 8 / 7 5 3 / 2 9 4. Mars (red panel; cream triangle holding a small square): 8 3 10 / 9 7 5 / 4 11 6. Row 3: Ketu (blue-violet panel; cream house-like shape with a flag point on the left and a pennant point on the right): 14 9 16 / 15 13 11 / 19 17 12 as printed. Saturn (navy panel; cream square frame): 12 7 14 / 13 11 9 / 8 15 10. Rahu (maroon panel; cream bell/tower shape with flared sides): 13 8 15 / 14 12 10 / 9 16 11. Row/column/diagonal sums (computed from the printed numbers): Mercury 24, Venus 30, Moon 18, Jupiter 27, Sun 15, Mars 21, Saturn 33, Rahu 36; Ketu would be 39.
unclear: Ketu's bottom-left cell reads 19 in the picture (checked at high zoom). With 19 the Ketu rows sum to 39, 39, 48 and the first column to 48, so it is not a magic square; a magic square would need 10 there (10 + 17 + 12 = 39). Treat as a printed error in the book.
Name tags and the 3x3 numbers were read at high zoom; the decorative shapes (arrow, star, ring, rays, triangle, house, bell) are described approximately.

belongs_to: "Notice that a different magic sum is associated with each graha. A picture of a Kubera Yantra is shown below:"
description: Left: a square panel with a yellow background and the italic maroon title 'Kubera Yantra' at the top. Inside it, a maroon cross-shaped (plus-shaped) frame; inside that a brown ring, then a gold lotus-petal ring, a blue ring, and an inner brown disc with a gold six-pointed star (hexagram). At the very centre of the star is a tiny green 3 x 3 grid of numbers (too small to read). A thin black arrow starts at that tiny grid and points right to an enlarged 3 x 3 mint-green grid with dark outlines and numbers: row 1: 27, 20, 25; row 2: 22, 24, 26; row 3: 23, 28, 21 (every row, column and diagonal adds to 72).

belongs_to: "Here are some possibilities:" - rhythms of short and long syllables for 8 beats
description: Four left-aligned lines of words, a vertical ellipsis (three dots) under them. LONG is printed in bold, SHORT in regular type: line 1: 'long long long long' (all bold); line 2: 'short short short short short short short short' (8 words, all regular); line 3: 'short long long short long' (the three 'long' bold); line 4: 'long long short short long' (the three 'long' bold). Each line is 8 beats (short = 1 beat, long = 2 beats). Plain text, but the bold type carries the meaning.

belongs_to: "Here are all the ways of writing each of the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4, as the sum of 1's and 2's."
description: A table with red outline and red lines, 3 columns. Header row (light peach fill, bold): first cell blank | 'Different Ways' | 'Number of Ways'. Rows (white): n = 1 | '1' | 1 ; n = 2 | '1 + 1' and '2' (two lines in the cell) | 2 ; n = 3 | '1 + 1 + 1', '1 + 2', '2 + 1' (three lines) | 3 ; n = 4 | '1 + 1 + 1 + 1', '1 + 1 + 2', '1 + 2 + 1', '2 + 1 + 1', '2 + 2' (five lines) | 5. The 'n =' entries are italic n. The table continues on the next page with the row n = 5 (see P15-table-1).

belongs_to: "Here is a systematic way to write down all rhythms of short and long syllables having 5 beats. Write a '1+' in front of all rhythms having 4 beats, and then a '2+' in front of all rhythms having 3 beats." (continuation of the table of page 14)
description: Top of page 15: one more table row (red outline, red lines, white cells, no header repeated) with three cells: 'n = 5' (italic n) | left cell with 5 lines: '1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1', '1 + 1 + 1 + 2', '1 + 1 + 2 + 1', '1 + 2 + 1 + 1', '1 + 2 + 2' | right cell with 3 lines: '2 + 1 + 1 + 1', '2 + 1 + 2', '2 + 2 + 1'. The left list is the 5 rhythms starting with 1+ and the right list the 3 rhythms starting with 2+; 5 + 3 = 8. No separate 'Number of Ways' number is printed in this row.

belongs_to: "So, how many rhythms of short and long syllables are there having 8 beats? We simply take the 8th element of the Virahanka sequence:"
description: One line of text: '1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, ...' in which the number 34 (the 8th term) has a light-pink/red highlight box behind it; all other numbers are plain.

belongs_to: "How many petals do you see on each of these flowers?" - three daisy pictures with captions
description: Three flower pictures side by side, flower heads seen from the front with a short green stem at the bottom, each with an italic caption below: left: yellow flower with a dark brown centre, caption 'A daisy with 13 petals' (13 separate petals counted all round); middle: larger, lighter yellow flower with a reddish-brown centre and overlapping petals, caption 'A daisy with 21 petals'; right: pale blue-white daisy with a golden-orange centre and many overlapping petals, caption 'A daisy with 34 petals'.
unclear: Petal counts of the 21-petal and 34-petal flowers could not be verified by counting because the petals overlap; the numbers 21 and 34 are the printed captions. Only the 13-petal flower was counted (13).

belongs_to: Page art under the drumming children, before "6.5 Digits in Disguise" (matches the 8-beat rhythms of P14-pattern-1)
description: Three rows of rounded, hand-drawn-looking dashes, all the same total length. Row 1: 4 long dashes: dark blue, light blue, dark blue, light blue. Row 2: 8 short dashes: teal, teal, purple, purple, teal, teal, purple, purple. Row 3: short purple, long dark blue, long light blue, short teal, long dark blue (short, long, long, short, long). A long dash is twice the width of a short dash, so each row is 8 beats (long = 2, short = 1). Decorative page art next to the drum picture; the children playing drums (a girl, a boy and a man with tabla drums) are decoration and not listed.
